mathgap.title: Sequential Transfer Application
mathgap.principle: Process each "X gives N to Y" statement in the order it appears, immediately subtracting N from X and adding N to Y. Subsequent statements refer to the updated counts. Skipping this step leaves later equations using stale values.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever the problem contains a "gives" transfer before any later count or comparison statements.
mathgap.example: Ignoring the order of a transfer and using the original counts for a later "A has N potatoes" constraint, causing A’s count to be off by the transferred amount.

mathgap.title: Signed Interpretation of "has K more than"
mathgap.principle: A statement "A has K more potatoes than B" translates to A − B = K, i.e. A = B + K. Do not swap the two names; the first name is the larger one.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a comparative statement of the form "X has K more than Y" appears.
mathgap.example: Interpreting "Reta has 9 more potatoes than Jonathan" as Jonathan = Reta + 9, which flips the intended direction.

mathgap.title: Signed Equality for Difference Statements
mathgap.principle: For a sentence like "The number of potatoes that A has more than B is equal to the difference between the number of potatoes that C and D have", write (A − B) = (C − D). Preserve the order of names on each side; do not replace the expression with absolute values.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement equates a "has more than" difference to another "difference between" pair.
mathgap.example: Treating "The number of potatoes that Teddy has more than Arie is equal to the difference between the number of potatoes that Loren and Shaquan have" as |Teddy − Arie| = |Loren − Shaquan|, losing sign information.

mathgap.title: Signed Interpretation of "difference between X and Y"
mathgap.principle: The phrase "difference between the number of X and Y" should be read as X − Y, preserving the order given, not as an absolute distance. This allows the expression to be negative when the narrative dictates it.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement mentions "difference between the number of X and Y".
mathgap.example: Interpreting "difference between the number of potatoes that Norene and Michelle have" as |Norene − Michelle| instead of Norene − Michelle.

mathgap.title: Current‑Count Constraint for "has N"
mathgap.principle: A statement "A has N potatoes" constrains A’s count at that point in the narrative, i.e. after any earlier transfers have been applied. It is not necessarily the initial amount before any transfers.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a direct count statement appears after one or more transfer statements.
mathgap.example: Assuming "Tina has 22 potatoes" is her starting amount and then also adding the 15 she receives from Britt, double‑counting the transfer.

mathgap.title: Iterative Substitution and Propagation
mathgap.principle: Whenever a variable’s value becomes known, substitute it into all pending equations and recompute any other variables that become solvable. This step‑by‑step reduction prevents the system from staying under‑determined.
mathgap.when_to_apply: After solving any equation that yields a concrete number for a person.
mathgap.example: Finding Reta = Jonathan + 9 but never plugging that relation into the later equality involving Jonathan and Reta, leaving the system incomplete.

mathgap.title: Allow Negative Differences in Contradictory "more than" Phrases
mathgap.principle: When a "more than" phrase appears on the left side of an equality that contradicts a previous comparative statement, treat the resulting difference as possibly negative. Do not enforce that every "A has more than B" must be positive in that context.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When paired statements like "Hayes has 9 more than Mason" and "The number of potatoes that Mason has more than Hayes is equal to …" occur.
mathgap.example: Assuming Mason − Hayes must be positive, which makes the second equation impossible, instead of recognizing it yields a negative value.

mathgap.title: Consistency Check After Solving
mathgap.principle: After obtaining values for all variables, verify each original statement—including transfers, direct counts, and difference equations—holds true. If any fails, revisit sign interpretations or the order of operations.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Immediately before outputting the final answer.
mathgap.example: Deriving a solution where Britt’s final count is negative after giving 15 potatoes, indicating a mis‑applied transfer or sign error.

mathgap.description: Swapped direction in "has K more than" statements
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model focuses on the phrase "more than" and mistakenly assumes the second name is the larger one.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Remember that "A has K more than B" means A = B + K; keep the first name as the larger quantity.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model assumes "difference" always denotes a non‑negative distance.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Preserve the order of names and interpret "difference between X and Y" as X − Y, even if the result is negative.

mathgap.description: Ignoring the chronological order of transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model treats all "gives" statements as simultaneous or applies them after processing other constraints.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Process each transfer as it appears, updating the giver’s and receiver’s counts before evaluating later statements.

mathgap.description: Treating "has N" as an initial count regardless of position
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model assumes every direct count refers to the starting state, not the current state after earlier transfers.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Interpret a "has N" statement as a constraint on the current count at that point in the narrative, after any prior transfers.

mathgap.description: Assuming all "more than" differences must be positive
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model expects "more than" to always indicate a positive gap and rejects negative results.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Allow the signed difference (first minus second) to be negative when the surrounding equations dictate it.
